---
title: "11. Rolling Deployments"
description: "Upgrade servers in batches without closing the stand: serial, max_fail_percentage, any_errors_fatal, delegate_to, run_once, throttle, strategies, health checks, and the maths of batches and failure thresholds."
---

## The problem

Version 1.1.0 of the Lemonade app is ready. If you upgrade `web1` and `web2` **at the same time**, both reload together and customers see errors for a moment. Worse: if 1.1.0 is broken, **both** servers are broken, and the stand is closed.

You want to:

1. take one server out of the load balancer,
2. upgrade it,
3. check that it really works,
4. put it back,
5. then move to the next server, and **stop** at the first failure.

## Explain it like I'm ten

::: {.callout-tip title="Swapping football players"}
In a football match the coach never takes all the players off at once. That would leave the pitch empty and the other team would score. Instead the coach makes **substitutions**: one player comes off, a fresh player goes on, and the team keeps playing the whole time.

If the new player twists an ankle in the first minute, the coach stops making substitutions and thinks again.

A rolling deployment is a substitution plan for servers. `serial: 1` means "swap one server at a time". `max_fail_percentage: 0` means "if any new player gets hurt, stop the substitutions".
:::

## The concept, precisely

- Normally a play runs each task on **all** its hosts before moving to the next task.
- With `serial`, Ansible splits the hosts into **batches** and runs the **whole play** on one batch before starting the next. In the output, the `PLAY [...]` header repeats once per batch.
- After each task, Ansible checks the share of failed hosts in the current batch. If it is above `max_fail_percentage`, the whole run stops, and later batches are never touched.
- Tasks that act on **another** machine, such as a load balancer, use `delegate_to`.
- Notified handlers run at the end of each section **in each batch**, so a server is reloaded before its health check.

## Every rolling-update keyword

| Keyword | What it does | Rule / convention | Example |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| `serial: N` | Batches of N hosts. | `1` is the safest; the last batch may be smaller. | `serial: 1` |
| `serial: "P%"` | Batches of P percent of the play's hosts. | Rounded **down**, but at least 1 host. | `serial: "30%"` |
| `serial: [a, b, c]` | Growing batches: first `a`, then `b`, then `c` for the rest. | The last value repeats until all hosts are done. Classic canary: `[1, "30%", "100%"]`. | `serial: [1, 5, 10]` |
| `max_fail_percentage` | Stop when the failed share of a batch is **greater than** this. | `0` stops at the first failure. | `max_fail_percentage: 0` |
| `any_errors_fatal` | Stop the play on all hosts as soon as any host fails. | Works with or without `serial`. The failing task finishes on the current batch, then nothing else runs. | `any_errors_fatal: true` |
| `delegate_to` | Run this task on another host, with the current host's variables. | For load balancers, monitoring and DNS. | `delegate_to: lb1` |
| `run_once` | Run the task on one host only, **once per batch**. | Combine with `delegate_to` for one-off work. | `run_once: true` |
| `throttle` | At most N hosts run this task at the same time. | Cannot go above `forks` or `serial`. | `throttle: 1` |
| `strategy: linear` | Every host finishes a task before the next task starts. | The default. Required for `max_fail_percentage`. | `strategy: linear` |
| `strategy: free` | Each host runs at its own speed. | Faster, but `max_fail_percentage` is not supported. | `strategy: free` |
| `order` | Which hosts go first. | `inventory`, `sorted`, `reverse_sorted`, `reverse_inventory`, `shuffle`. | `order: sorted` |
| `ansible_play_batch` | Magic variable: the hosts in this batch. | | `{{ ansible_play_batch }}` |

### The health-check modules

| Module | What it waits for | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `ansible.builtin.wait_for` | A port to open or close, or text to appear in a file. | `wait_for: { port: 8080, timeout: 30 }` |
| `ansible.builtin.uri` + `until` | An HTTP status, retried. | `until: health.status == 200` ([lesson 8](08-conditionals-loops-and-handlers.qmd)) |

## Worked example

The heart of the lab's [`rolling-update.yml`](examples/rolling-update.yml) is the play header:

```yaml
- name: Upgrade the web servers one at a time
  hosts: web
  gather_facts: false
  serial: 1                  # one server per batch
  max_fail_percentage: 0     # any failure stops the rollout
```

And the drain → upgrade → check → enable pattern, written as `pre_tasks`, `roles` and `post_tasks`. (The full file also has a first pre-task, "Create the load balancer folder", with `run_once: true`, and a last post-task that removes the `.off` file.)

```yaml
  pre_tasks:
    - name: Take this server out of the load balancer
      ansible.builtin.file: { path: "{{ lab_root }}/lb/{{ inventory_hostname }}.off", state: touch }
      delegate_to: localhost
  roles:
    - lemonade_web
  post_tasks:
    - name: Wait until the menu shows the new version
      ansible.builtin.wait_for:
        path: "{{ lab_root }}/{{ inventory_hostname }}/site/index.html"
        search_regex: "version {{ lemonade_version }}"
```

Run it:

```bash
ansible-playbook rolling-update.yml -e lemonade_version=1.1.0
```

Real output, trimmed. Notice that the `PLAY` header appears twice, once per batch:

```text
PLAY [Upgrade the web servers one at a time] ***********************************
TASK [Create the load balancer folder] *****************************************
changed: [web1 -> localhost]
TASK [Take this server out of the load balancer] *******************************
changed: [web1 -> localhost]
TASK [lemonade_web : Render the menu page] *************************************
changed: [web1]
RUNNING HANDLER [lemonade_web : Reload nginx] **********************************
ok: [web1] =>
    msg: nginx reloaded on web1
TASK [Wait until the menu shows the new version] *******************************
ok: [web1]
TASK [Put this server back into the load balancer] *****************************
changed: [web1 -> localhost]

PLAY [Upgrade the web servers one at a time] ***********************************
TASK [Create the load balancer folder] *****************************************
ok: [web2 -> localhost]
...
PLAY RECAP *********************************************************************
web1   : ok=8    changed=4    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
web2   : ok=8    changed=3    unreachable=0    failed=0    skipped=0    rescued=0    ignored=0
```

Three things to see:

- `web1 -> localhost` means the task ran on the control node (the "load balancer") on behalf of `web1`.
- The handler ran **inside** the batch, before the health check.
- "Create the load balancer folder" has `run_once: true`, yet it ran in **both** batches: `changed` for `web1`, then `ok` for `web2`. `run_once` means once per batch.

**Dry run first.** `--check --diff` shows the version change and skips `wait_for`, which cannot be predicted:

```text
-<p>Served by web1, version 1.1.0</p>
+<p>Served by web1, version 1.2.0</p>
changed: [web1]
TASK [Wait until the menu shows the new version] *******************************
skipping: [web1]
```

**On real servers** the drain step talks to the real load balancer, and the check calls the app:

```yaml
- name: Drain this server in HAProxy
  community.general.haproxy: { state: disabled, host: "{{ inventory_hostname }}", backend: lemonade }
  delegate_to: lb1
- name: Wait for the app's health endpoint
  ansible.builtin.uri: { url: "http://{{ ansible_host }}:8080/health" }
  register: health
  until: health.status == 200
  retries: 10
  delay: 3
```

## Rules and conventions

- **Keep the version in Git** (`group_vars/web.yml`), not only in `-e`. Otherwise the next `site.yml` run puts the default version back. You can see this in the lab: after a rolling update with `-e lemonade_version=1.1.0`, a plain `site.yml --check` wants to change the menu back to 1.0.0.
- **Drain, upgrade, verify, enable**, in that order, every time.
- **Start small**: `serial: [1, "30%", "100%"]` upgrades one canary server first.
- **Fail fast**: `max_fail_percentage: 0` for web servers; consider `any_errors_fatal: true` for database schema changes.
- **Health checks must test the app**, not just the port. A port can be open while the app returns errors.
- **Leave headroom**: never take out more servers than the rest can carry (see the maths below).

## Common mistakes

| Mistake | Symptom | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| No `serial` | All web servers reload at once; brief outage. | `serial: 1` or a percentage. |
| `max_fail_percentage: 50` with `serial: 2` | One failed server in a batch of two does **not** stop the run (50% is not above 50). | Use `0`, or `49` if you want "stop at 1 of 2". |
| `strategy: free` with `max_fail_percentage` | Warning: not supported with the free strategy. | Use the default `linear` strategy. |
| `run_once` expecting "once per play" with `serial` | The task runs once in every batch. | Move it into its own play without `serial`. |
| Enabling the server before the health check | A broken server receives traffic. | The health check must come before "put back". |
| Version only passed with `-e` | The next `site.yml` reverts the version. | Store it in `group_vars`. |

## Mathematical Abstraction

**Batch sizes.** Let the play have $N$ hosts and `serial` the list $s_1, s_2, \dots, s_m$. Each entry becomes a batch size:

$$
b_j =
\begin{cases}
\max\!\left(1, \left\lfloor \dfrac{q_j}{100} \cdot N \right\rfloor\right) & \text{if } s_j \text{ is a percentage } q_j\% \\[1ex]
s_j & \text{if } s_j \text{ is a number}
\end{cases}
\qquad j = 1, 2, \dots
$$

where:

- $N$ is the number of hosts the play targets;
- $s_j$ is the $j$-th entry of the `serial` list, and $q_j$ is its value when written as a percentage;
- $\lfloor x \rfloor$ rounds down;
- $b_j$ is the size of batch $j$; after the list ends, the last entry is used again; the final batch takes whatever hosts remain, so it can be smaller.

**Example 1**, the lab: $N = 2$, `serial: 1`. So $b_1 = 1$, $b_2 = 1$: two batches, `web1` then `web2`.

**Example 2**, a summer fleet of $N = 10$ web servers with `serial: [1, "30%", "100%"]`:

- $b_1 = 1$ (one canary);
- $b_2 = \max(1, \lfloor 0.30 \cdot 10 \rfloor) = \max(1, 3) = 3$;
- $b_3 = \max(1, \lfloor 1.00 \cdot 10 \rfloor) = 10$, but only $10 - 1 - 3 = 6$ hosts remain, so the batch has 6.

Batches of 1, 3 and 6. A real run on ten test hosts printed exactly `['w01']`, then `['w02', 'w03', 'w04']`, then `['w05', …, 'w10']`.

**When the run stops.** After each task, Ansible compares the failed share of the batch with the limit:

$$
\frac{F}{B} > \frac{p}{100} \;\Rightarrow\; \text{stop the whole run}
$$

where:

- $B$ is the size of the current batch;
- $F$ is the number of hosts in that batch that have failed;
- $p$ is `max_fail_percentage`, from 0 to 100;
- the comparison is **strictly greater than**: hitting the limit exactly is still allowed.

**Example 1**: $B = 4$, $p = 25$, and one host fails. $F/B = 1/4 = 0.25$, which is **not** greater than $0.25$, so the run continues. A real test did exactly that.

**Example 2**: $B = 4$, $p = 25$, two hosts fail. $2/4 = 0.5 > 0.25$, so the run stops. The real test printed `NO MORE HOSTS LEFT` and never started the next batch.

**Example 3**, the lab: $p = 0$. Any failure gives $F/B \ge 1/B > 0$, so the first broken server stops the rollout.

**Capacity during the rollout.** While a batch is drained, the rest of the fleet carries the traffic:

$$
\text{capacity} = \frac{N - b}{N}
$$

where $N$ is the number of web servers and $b$ the size of the batch currently drained.

**Example.** The lab: $N = 2$ and $b = 1$, so capacity is $(2 - 1)/2 = 50\%$. If the stand's peak traffic needs 70% of both servers, a Saturday-noon rollout would overload `web2`. Roll out in a quiet hour, or add a third server: $(3 - 1)/3 \approx 67\%$. For the summer fleet, the 6-host batch leaves $(10 - 6)/10 = 40\%$, so a large last batch should only be used when traffic is low.
